slide.title: Physical Therapy Personal Statement Examples
slide.sub: 3 PTCAS essays, with notes on what makes each one work

segments.say: Here are three physical therapy personal statement examples for PTCAS, with notes on what makes each one work. We wrote them as teaching models, so the applicants are invented. All three come from our page of six PT examples, which is linked in the description.

slide.label: The PTCAS prompt
slide.text: As a prospective Doctor of Physical Therapy, how do you see yourself having an impact on the profession upon entering the field?
slide.foot: 4,500 characters, spaces included. Every program reads the same essay.

segments.say: First, the prompt. PTCAS asks how you see yourself having an impact on the profession once you enter the field. It suggests practice, education, research, leadership, or community work. The essay is limited to 4,500 characters, spaces included, and every program you apply to reads the same essay, so leave school names out of it.
Example one comes from an applicant who has taught adaptive skiing for four winters.

slide.label: Example 1 · The opening
slide.text: The first time I helped a student transfer from his wheelchair into a bi-ski, I did most of it wrong.
slide.hl: I did most of it wrong.

segments.say: The essay opens with a mistake. The ski creeps downhill during a transfer, and the student finally tells the applicant to hold it still and stop talking. Starting with something you got wrong shows you learning from a patient, and readers trust that more than an opening about how inspiring the work was.

slide.label: Example 1 · Details a reader can check
items: Hips centered in the bucket
Pressure relief for skin
Boot checks for skiers who can't feel their feet

segments.say: The details are ones a reader can check: hips centered in the bucket, pressure relief, and boot checks for skiers who can't feel their feet. They tell the reader this applicant has done the work for years.

slide.label: Example 1 · What they can't do yet
slide.text: I can tell when a student is tired or cold, but I can't assess why someone's trunk control is poor.
slide.hl: I can't assess why someone's trunk control is poor.

segments.say: Right before the ending, the applicant says what they can't do yet. They can tell when a student is tired or cold, but they can't assess trunk control, or tell which muscles still work after an incomplete injury. That shows the reader what the degree would add.

slide.label: Example 1 · How it answers the prompt
items: Make recreation part of discharge planning
Rewrite volunteer transfer training with former patients

segments.say: Then the last paragraph answers the prompt with two plans: make recreation part of discharge planning, and rewrite the volunteer transfer training with former patients. Both come from things the applicant saw on the mountain, so they read as real goals and not a list of the prompt's categories.

segments.chapter: Example 2: Army medic and rehab tech
segments.say: Example two comes from a former Army medic who now works as a rehab tech on an inpatient unit.

slide.label: Example 2 · The opening
slide.text: "I am going to black out and hit my head."

segments.say: It opens with a patient's words: I am going to black out and hit my head. He is recovering from pneumonia and won't stand. His strength is coming back, and fear is what keeps him in the chair. The rest of the essay keeps returning to that problem.

slide.label: Example 2 · What the PT did
items: Checked his orthostatic vitals
Had him stand for ten seconds, then sit
Walked a few steps beside him, with rests

segments.say: The applicant describes how the physical therapist got him up. She checked his orthostatic vitals, had him stand for ten seconds and sit back down, then walked a few steps beside him. Admissions readers look for this in observation hours. It shows you watched how the result happened, not only that it happened.

slide.label: Example 2 · Communication you can see
slide.b: "Tell me what you are going to do when you get home."
slide.b_note: shows what the patient took in

segments.say: This contrast turns a claim about communication into something the reader can see. Do you understand gets a polite yes. Tell me what you are going to do when you get home shows what the patient took in.

slide.label: Example 2 · How it answers the prompt
items: Teach nurses and techs which patients are safe to walk
A daily mobility goal on each room's whiteboard
Work with veterans, ideally at a VA hospital

segments.say: The impact paragraph starts from a detail in the story: the patient saw a PT for about thirty minutes a day. So the applicant wants to teach nurses and techs which patients are safe to walk, and to post a daily mobility goal in each room. The VA goal comes with a reason only this applicant could give. Veterans often say they are fine when they aren't, and that matters when you are deciding whether someone is safe to stand.

segments.chapter: Example 3: Caregiver for a parent with Parkinson's

slide.title: Caregiver for a parent with Parkinson's

segments.say: Example three comes from an applicant who helped care for a parent with Parkinson's, then worked as a rehab aide.

slide.label: Example 3 · The opening
slide.text: Physical therapy found me in my mom's kitchen.

segments.say: It opens with one short line: physical therapy found me in my mom's kitchen. The details that follow show Parkinson's through daily life: grocery lists with smaller and smaller letters, freezing in doorways, and tape on a step she kept missing.

slide.label: Example 3 · A lesson before any PT appeared
slide.text: When she froze, I learned to give one direction at a time and then wait, since saying "come on, come on" only made it worse.
slide.hl: give one direction at a time and then wait

segments.say: The applicant learned something before any physical therapist appeared: give one direction and wait, because come on, come on made the freezing worse. That detail comes back at the end as the reason for one of the plans.

slide.label: Example 3 · Proof it's about the field
items: Volunteered at a neuro rehab center
Worked part-time as a rehab aide
Saw patients do a task in therapy and still struggle at home

segments.say: Personal stories raise a question for readers: is this interest about the field, or about one person? This applicant answers it with time at a neuro rehab center and a job as a rehab aide, and by reporting a pattern from that work. Patients could do a task in therapy and still struggle at home.

slide.label: Example 3 · How it answers the prompt
items: Caregiver sessions through Parkinson's support groups
Home visits
A weekly community exercise class between rounds of therapy

segments.say: The plans fill gaps this family ran into: short caregiver sessions through Parkinson's support groups, home visits, and a weekly community exercise class for the months between rounds of therapy.

slide.label: What all three do
items: Open with a specific moment
Show what a PT did, step by step
Name what you can't do yet
Answer the prompt with plans from your own story

segments.say: All three examples do the same four things. They open with a specific moment. They show what a physical therapist did, step by step. They name what the applicant can't do yet. And they answer the prompt with plans that come from the applicant's own story.
